title: When bird flu hit the UK, suffering seabirds died in their thousands. Australia’s wild flocks will soon do the same
summary: Australia’s bird population will experience ‘large mortalities’ and risk species loss, modelling based on global outbreaks shows
body: Sandwich terns are a graceful seabird known for their committed, forceful and spectacular plunging dives into the ocean to catch fish. Thousands of the species started to fall sick across Europe in 2022 with tens of thousands dying as a lineage of the H5N1 bird flu – 2.3.4.4b – spread through the continent’s wild flocks. The effects of the virus on the brain cause the terns to flounder on the ground, craning and straining their necks in a suffering behaviour known as star-gazing. It is difficult to watch. “I remember a colony at Scolt Head Island in Norfolk,” says Prof James Pearce-Higgins, the director of science at the British Trust for Ornithology. “You had adult terns trying to mate with dead terns and chicks begging for food from their dying parents. “It was a real sense of a colony collapse as you watched this transfer of the virus between birds.” Sandwich terns are close relatives of greater crested terns, which are seen all around Australia and were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from the disease in Australia on South Australia’s Limestone Coast. Since the virus re-emerged in Europe in 2021 it has swept over every other continent, killing millions of birds and mammals, and infecting more than 400 bird species as well as mammals – in particular, seals and sea lions. The virus was finally detected in Australia two months ago in migratory seabirds that likely brought the disease from breeding grounds in the subantarctic. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email This week, the federal government revealed analysis of the potential threat to Australia’s wildlife which showed almost 400 species of birds and mammals were at “high risk” or worse if they caught the disease. One expert who worked on the analysis, Prof John Woinarski of Charles Darwin University, tells the Guardian he expects the disease will have spread across the continent within a year. Pearce-Higgins says: “I would expect Australia is going to experience large mortalities, like those we have been through, and it’s going to put some species at risk.” Almost half of Australia’s bird species are unique to the continent, meaning that a lot of uncertainty comes with predicting what H5N1 could do to the animal population. It also means the risk of the virus causing planet-wide extinctions is higher now that every continent is affected. Death toll will be ‘confronting’ “We’ve been looking overseas since 2021 and seeing the advance of this virus,” says Dr Sara Ryding, an evolutionary ecologist at Deakin University. “It has been horrible overseas – tens of thousands of birds dying in single colonies. “The concern was, we knew it was going to arrive eventually – how could it not? But we didn’t know what it would look like when it got here.” Ryding has led research to project the level of risk from H5N1 for all Australia’s bird families by developing a model based on official reports of the disease from around the globe to the World Organisation for Animal Health. The research suggested the most at-risk families of birds were gannets and boobies (Sulidae), followed in descending order of risk by cranes (Gruidae), darters (Anhingidae), ducks, geese and swans (Anatidae), and gulls, terns and noddies (Laridae). But a host of other bird families – including pelicans, crows, ravens, falcons and kestrels – were all predicted to be susceptible. While many species of those birds are not considered threatened, the sight of large numbers of dead and sick birds, particularly larger species like swans and pelicans, “is going to be confronting,” Ryding says. “I don’t want to cause panic, but we have seen the devastation it has caused overseas and there’s no reason to think it will be any less devastating here,” she says. “I think it will be really bad.” Studies have identified several behaviours that can make animals susceptible to catching the disease, such as scavenging dead and dying animals for food (as do gulls and Tasmanian devils), spending time in dense colonies (like seals and waterbirds) and spending time around bodies of water where the virus can live for weeks or months, or where other infected animals might also be around. ‘Devastating’ for seals and sea lions The virus has been particularly damaging for seals and sea lions. Tens of thousands of seals and sea lions have died in outbreaks in Peru, Chile, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina and, most recently, on Australia’s subantarctic islands of Heard and McDonald. The virus can cause debilitating conditions for the seals and sea lions – known collectively as pinnipeds – with severe neurological and respiratory symptoms. Australia has three resident pinniped species – the New Zealand fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the already endangered Australian sea lion – and government analysis has suggested the risk for all three from the virus is “very high”, meaning “very severe reduction in population size or viability is predicted” if the virus reaches them. Dr Saia Bartes is an Argentinian marine biologist who has just completed her PhD on Australian fur seals at Deakin University and has helped study declines in South American sea lions after the virus struck there. “It was devastating for them. In north Patagonia, we lost a third of the sea lions,” she says. Because pinnipeds often share space with infected birds, and tend to be in tightly packed groups, Bartes says they are particularly susceptible. Pinniped numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting, she says, and “they could start declining again really quickly, which is happening in South America” if the virus found them. Back in the UK, Pearce-Higgins says there is some hope. Their experience of collaboration with conservation groups, volunteers and local authorities through weekly and later monthly meetings had been critical in the response. And there were some signs the impacts of the virus may be slowing. “The hope is that because a lot of these birds are long-lived, the population could be more resilient. But we still don’t really know the probabilities of future outbreaks,” he says. “It might look really bad for a few years, but the hope is that [Australia] can focus on the conservation of what is left.”

title: Fears of ‘catastrophic’ decline of giant Australian cuttlefish after only 44 counted in dive survey
summary: Calls for South Australian government to release official estimates for cuttlefish, which once numbered in hundreds of thousands in upper Spencer Gulf
body: Scientists and divers have called on the South Australian government to release official cuttlefish population estimates amid fears of a “catastrophic” decline, after a dive survey counted only 44 individuals. Each year, tens to hundreds of thousands of giant Australian cuttlefish assemble off the coast of Whyalla, in the upper Spencer Gulf, to breed – the only place globally where cuttlefish gather en masse. In surveys dating back to 1998, populations ranged from a low of 13,500 in 2013 to a high of 247,000 in 2020. More than 63,000 were recorded in 2025. Numbers this year were widely expected to be the lowest on record, after the devastating effects of the toxic algal bloom on the state’s marine environment. The team of four divers from ecological not-for-profit Eyrelab, who surveyed the coastline in July, also counted only 440 eggs where there would normally be millions. “This is by far the lowest abundance that we’ve had on record,” said Manny Katz, diver and Eyrelab director, who added that the few dozen cuttlefish they saw were “not out and about – they’re hiding”. Stefan Andrews, a marine biologist from the Great Southern Reef Foundation, called for the state government to release the official figures. “It’s clear that it’s going to be bad news,” he said. “People need to know just how bad the situation is. “Let’s see it, and not sit on it too long because the clock is actually ticking.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The historically low numbers led tourism and dive operators in Whyalla to cancel their cuttlefish season in June. On 1 July, the state government introduced temporary restrictions on recreational activities such as swimming and snorkelling, to minimise disturbance to breeding cuttlefish and help protect their eggs and hatchlings. At a press conference on 30 June, Prof Mike Steer, the SA Research and Development Institute’s executive director, said “less than 50 animals” had been observed earlier in the season. Those were “raw counts”, he said, with further monitoring and analysis required before providing a population estimate. A state government spokesperson said surveys had now been completed, and 2026 estimates would be released after review. “Cuttlefish numbers naturally rise and fall from year to year”, driven by environmental conditions, the spokesperson said. “The algal bloom reached the giant Australian cuttlefish breeding site at Point Lowly in upper Spencer Gulf and, while it appears likely the algal bloom has impacted cuttlefish numbers, researchers are working to determine whether this contributed to the reduced population.” Assoc Prof Zoe Doubleday, a cuttlefish and octopus expert at Adelaide University, said the bloom may have killed cuttlefish directly or changed the availability of their food supply – or their predators’ food supply. Cuttlefish live short lives and adults usually die after breeding, making the population heavily dependent on the success of each breeding season. Australia’s first bloom of toxic Karenia cristata algae, which began in March last year, is still present along parts of the South Australian coastline. It is the largest and most destructive algal bloom in the nation’s history. The latest testing results show elevated levels of Karenia algae at seven of 32 testing sites on the Eyre peninsula, and two of 19 sites on the Yorke peninsula. Andrews said the federal government should also assess listing the species as threatened under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, given the “catastrophic decline” in numbers. While giant cuttlefish were found along the Australian coast, the animals in the upper Spencer Gulf were genetically distinct, he said. In addition to their globally unique aggregation, the animals displayed distinct behaviours, such as female mimicry – “males pretending to be female, to get up close to the other females so then they can sneak mate with them”.

title: Hospitality recruitment app Supp calls gig-workers contractors. Some users say it leads to casual work without entitlements
summary: Exclusive: Workers’ rights experts raise ‘alarm bells’ over app requiring ABNs for jobs they say lack worker autonomy
body: Concerns have been raised that workers using an increasingly popular Australian hospitality gig-work app may be missing out on entitlements such as superannuation by being hired as “independent contractors”, similar to delivery riders. Launched in Melbourne in 2017, Supp describes itself as a “jobs marketplace”, where hospitality businesses can advertise available shifts to potential workers at an hourly rate, and where workers can secure ad-hoc employment. It was created by Kate and Cameron Reid, the owners of Lune Croissanterie, who maintain a financial stake in the company but are no longer on its board. It has since expanded across Australia and the US, with the company claiming it was used by about 15,000 venues and 200,000 workers. Businesses pay workers through the app, with Supp adding a 12% surcharge as its service fee and sending workers payment advice and summaries at the end of the financial year. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email But Supp requires workers to have their own ABN, and describes them as individual contractors – not casual employees – to the hospitality businesses that hire them through the platform. Supp has rejected any suggestion that it has misrepresented the working relationship facilitated through the app. But concerns have been raised by a worker, Daniel McBurnie, who began investigating whether he was entitled to superannuation for shifts obtained through the app from 2021. Those shifts – including bartending, popcorn-selling, front-of-house and table-waiting – involved the same kinds of labour McBurnie said he had previously performed in hospitality. McBurnie said he was hired as an individual contractor – rather than a casual employee – for 15 different companies through Supp. He said he was never paid superannuation for any of those shifts, and that there was no mechanism within the app for businesses to collect that information or for him to provide it. “Hospitality workers coming in to do a barista shift – they don’t have autonomy,” McBurnie said. “They’re not setting their [pay] rate, they’re not setting their hours. They are reporting to a supervisor, they’re carrying out the tasks delegated to them.” Supp rejects ‘sham contracting’ allegations Casual employees have more workplace entitlements than independent contractors, including minimum rates of pay and casual loading, penalty rates, rest breaks, superannuation, and protection from unfair dismissal. There are also more obligations on employers, such as record-keeping requirements. Independent contractors who are paid mainly for their labour are also entitled to receive superannuation, according to the Australian Tax Office. There have also been moves to provide other entitlements for gig-workers, such as in the food delivery sector. McBurnie was worried the app could enable widespread misclassification of casual workers as independent contractors, and that hundreds of thousands of workers may be missing out on workplace entitlements and protections as a result. Misrepresenting an employment relationship as an independent contracting relationship – known as “sham contracting” – is unlawful under the Fair Work Act and can attract penalties of up to $546,000 for large businesses. Third parties involved in contraventions can also be liable. Supp’s chief executive, Jordan Murray, said the company rejected and denied “any suggestions and/or allegations made or raised in relation to misrepresentation of the working relationship arranged through Supp” and “any sham contracting allegations.” “Supp engages constructively with regulators and supports clear, workable standards for independent work on digital platforms,” Murray said. “As the law evolves we will keep adapting the platform with it, including tools that help businesses meet obligations where they apply.” The app’s co-founder, Cameron Reid, said: “Lune regularly uses Supp, and is confident to do so due to Supp’s regular legal compliance reviews, its diligent work with regulators, and the insurance and support offered to both sides of the marketplace.” ‘Deserves close scrutiny’ Imogen Szumer, a senior associate at law firm Maurice Blackburn, said the way Supp described the workplace relationship was “peculiar, looking at the type of work that this is”. “Just because the website or the app is saying that it’s an individual contractor relationship, doesn’t mean that it is. How the parties describe the relationship is one factor, but it is not determinative. And that’s obviously important in the employment relationship, which is inherently an unequal one,” Szumer said. “We have strict rules in this country governing the employment relationship and which provide important protections for employees. Where you have the business or the app provider saying that their arrangement falls outside the remit of our employment laws, that deserves close scrutiny.” Szumer said if workers showed up to shifts at times set by the business, used its tools and equipment, were subject to its control and direction the entire time, including complying with its policies, procedures and dress standard, “looking at all the circumstances, a court might find that, in actuality, the hospitality business is employing these workers on a casual basis.” Three other Supp users who spoke to Guardian Australia said they had not received superannuation or other entitlements. A Melbourne bartender, Fred Siggins, said he had taken on bartending work at events with a company that used Supp as a payment platform for ad-hoc roles. He did not receive superannuation for those shifts, but said it had not concerned him as he had been in a position to negotiate a high rate for the work. Miranda Roop used Supp to pick up bartending and front-of-house shifts after moving to Australia in November. The work was no different to roles she obtained through word-of-mouth or other means, she said, but in other circumstances she was usually brought on as a casual employee. “Hospo work is largely the same everywhere you go – with similar procedures and tasks,” she said. Another worker, who spoke to the Guardian on condition that his name not be published, said he had used Supp to find extra shifts intermittently between 2022 and 2025, mainly bartending and occasionally as a barista or server. He had not been paid superannuation for those shifts and assumed he would have to pay it himself. ‘Growing gigification’ McBurnie said the app was becoming “the new go-to” in hospitality. “You’ll see some venues that have used it literally thousands of times,” he said. But Pat O’Donnell, director of casino, pubs and clubs at the United Workers Union, said convenience for employers should not come at the expense of workers’ rights, security or fair treatment. “Alarm bells should ring whenever workers are told they need an ABN, or they must become a sole trader, to pick up a shift in a hospitality venue,” O’Donnell said. “United Workers Union is concerned by the growing gigification of hospitality work. Workers deserve secure jobs, fair pay and the protections that come with proper employment, not arrangements that shift risk on to workers to maximise flexibility for businesses.” McBurnie has called for the Fair Work Ombudsman to independently audit the platform and its use by businesses to source labour, saying many workers lacked the knowledge and confidence to take it on. “That is a more fair way to go about it rather than getting a really vulnerable section of the workforce to dispute their claims individually,” he said. The Fair Work Ombudsman refused to comment on Supp specifically, and encouraged workers with concerns to contact them or their union directly. • Do you have a story? Contact: stephanie.convery@theguardian.com

title: ‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn
summary: Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027
body: El Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn. Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). California has a 70%-100% chance of experiencing above-average rainfall along its coast, according to a model from the European center for medium-range forecasts. “El Niño is never going to guarantee any particular outcome in any California winter,” Daniel Swain, the UCLA climate scientist, noted at a virtual El Niño town hall hosted by the California state senator Mike McGuire this week. But, he added, a weather event as strong as the one being currently predicted shifts the odds in favor of a wet winter: “That will likely affect and increase the likelihood of coastal flooding, particularly during strong storm events or during king tide events.” California has been devastated by El Niños in the past. A 1982-83 weather system destroyed 33 oceanfront homes and damaged 3,000 other residences, according to the California coastal commission. In a 1997-98 El Niño, California experienced massive flooding and 17 storm-related deaths. In more recent history, during the El Niño winter of 2015-16, state officials reported record coastal erosion on California beaches. “With less beach in front of the coastline, the waves will have even greater impact on the shoreline with more likelihood of flooding and undercutting of cliffs,” said Mark Merrifield of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, at McGuire’s town hall. El Niño is not expected to completely erase drought in the US south-west, where some reservoirs are at an all-time low. “It would have to be exceptionally wet,” Dr Joel Lisonbee, senior associate scientist at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the Guardian in June. “That would also mean flooding, and the destruction and potential loss of life that comes along with that.” Swathes of the US Gulf coast and east coast, stretching from Florida up to the mid-Atlantic region, are facing similar high odds of increased precipitation. During El Niño years, central and south Florida has historically experienced more severe weather with more tornadoes and flood events, according to Noaa. In a 1998 El Niño winter, an outbreak of unusually strong tornadoes in that region led to 42 deaths and more than $100m in damage. Experts warn that not every El Niño behaves the same, nor does it affect different geographical regions in the same way. Some have fueled hurricanes and heavy precipitation, while others have triggered extreme heat and drought. While this is “a natural cycle”, Merrifield said at the town hall, the potential effects of a temporary sea-level rise in California from the super El Niño also “gives us a bit of a stress test of what the state is likely to experience with future climate change”. “The El Niño, I think, is a good opportunity to sort of see where our vulnerabilities are throughout the state and what we can do to prepare,” Merrifield added, “and it also is a sobering look at what we can expect with climate change.”

title: Blanche confirmation allows Trump to continue ‘pervasive, breathtaking corruption’, says Schumer – as it happened
summary: Senate minority leader condemns Republicans after Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer confirmed by 50 votes to 49 early on Saturday morning. This blog is now closed.
body: We’re wrapping our live politics coverage for the day. Here’s the top political news: The US Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general. Blanche, who was deputy attorney general prior to former AG Pam Bondi’s ouster, previously served as Donald Trump’s criminal defense attorney. Blanche won the confirmation by a 50-49 vote early Saturday morning. Just two Republican senators, Maine’s Susan Collins and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski, voted against him. Blanche was confirmed despite facing intense criticism for his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files. Remember: Trump’s Department of Justice was required by bipartisan legislation to disclose all files related to Epstein by 19 December, with redactions only in extremely limited circumstances. While some files were disclosed on this deadline, many were released after the congressionally mandated cutoff. Blanche’s rollout has also been criticized for redacting information that should have been public–-while disclosing survivors’ names. US Senators started their five-week recess this morning after handing Trump a major win with Blanche’s confirmation. But, GOP senators managed to go on recess without meeting some of Trump’s demands--including passage of the Save America Act. This proposed legislation would restrict voting across the US. Trump had pushed for senators to postpone their recess to green-light this act, but they reportedly told Trump portions of it would be included in a Republican budget package. It’s not just Blanche--dozens of Trump nominees were confirmed by the Senate early Saturday morning. Senate Republicans pushed through a resolution confirming more than 70 Trump picks for role such as ambassadors, judges, and US attorneys. Among the early morning votes pushed through the US Senate by Republicans before dawn was a resolution to confirm a slate of 71 of Donald Trump’s picks to serve in a variety of roles, including as ambassadors, US attorneys, judges and senior staff at federal agencies. One of the nominees confirmed this way was P Wells Griffith, a former Republican campaign operative and Trump aide who was the senior director for international energy and environment on the National Security Council in 2019. As of today, Griffith is now a US ambassador, representing the United States at the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna. The IAEA played a key role in verifying Iran’s compliance with the nuclear deal negotiated during the Obama administration, which Trump withdrew from during his first term, and could be similarly important should a new nuclear deal with Iran be struck by the Trump administration. During the impeachment inquiry over Trump’s pressure campaign against Ukraine in 2019, Fiona Hill, the NSC’s Russia expert during Trump’s first term, testified that Griffith was present at a July 2019 meeting with Ukrainian officials in which John Bolton, then Trump’s national security adviser, discovered that other US officials had secretly pressed Ukraine to open a sham investigation of Joe Biden. Griffith refused to testify to the House impeachment inquiry, defying a subpoena. Pete Buttigieg called for unity among Democrats on Friday during a rally in Michigan, saying “the stakes are high, and people from around the country, people from around the world, are watching” to see if Democrats can win the swing state. Buttigieg’s remarks, reported by Politico, came during a planned event that involved Michigan’s statewide Democratic ticket. Buttigieg ran for president in 2020 and is considered a possible Democratic contender for 2028. Michigan Democrats must hold onto their Senate seat if Democrats want to regain control of the Senate. And while Michigan has long been a battleground state, residents voted for Donald Trump in the last two elections, Politico noted. “We’re going to win because we know what it means to focus on what’s at stake, to lock arms as allies after a spirited primary, to pull together in common cause,” Buttigieg said. Buttigieg remained neutral during Michigan’s Senate primary, which exposed deep schisms within the Democratic party. Abdul El-Sayed won against the US representative Haley Stevens on Tuesday and is up against the Republican representative Mike Rogers in the general election. El-Sayed needs to attract moderate and establishment Democrats to win, Politico said, with the GOP noting a potential opportunity to attract some Democrats. “Wherever you sit, in this big tent of ours, and it is a big tent, but whatever corner of that tent you think of as home, there is a set of things, and I mean big, big things, where we agree with each other, we agree with most Michiganders, and Washington and Lansing Republicans disagree with us,” Buttigieg reportedly said. “That’s what’s at stake right now, and it’s not all about left, right and center, Democrat and Republican.” El-Sayed also called for coming together. “In the spirit of unity, in the spirit of the work, in the spirit of coming together, I want to thank both of my colleagues who ran, Haley Stevens and Mallory McMorrow, for an incredible race,” he reportedly said. “Their incredible public service in the state of Michigan, and I cannot wait to see what both of them will do next.” “They don’t know who we fight for,” he also said, referring to Republicans. “We fight for the families barely able to put their groceries in the cart and check out, we fight for the mom who’s worried about the childcare she needs to be able to work a job that barely pays enough, we fight for the folks who are afraid about what happens if they get sick. We fight for each other, and we don’t back down.” A former Republican strategist thinks that “this might be the year” that Democrats beat the GOP in a race for statewide office in Texas. Joseph Moreno’s comment came during an interview with Jake Tapper on CNN’s The Lead. Tapper questioned Moreno about the Texas state representative James Talarico besting the GOP state attorney general Ken Paxton 47-45% in recent polling. “It surprises me, and it worries me a little bit, Jake. Normally, I would say, ‘I’m not worried about this,’ right? It’s been 30 years since a Democrat won statewide office in Texas,” Moreno remarked, according to the Hill. Paxton beat the incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary after receiving Donald Trump’s endorsement. Talarico bested the Democrat representative Jasmine Crockett during the primary, his victory boosted by Democratic leaders, according to the Hill. “The problem is, here’s what happens – in 2024, the Republican was up by 2%, wins by 8%. In 2020, Cornyn was up 10%, wins by 10%,” Moreno said. “Now, you’ve got Talarico even, or maybe even ahead of Paxton.” “I hate to say it, this might be the year for Democrats in Texas,” Moreno also remarked. US senators kicked off their five-week recess early on Saturday after delivering Donald Trump a major victory – but punting several of the president’s demands. Senators confirmed Trump’s pick for US attorney general, Todd Blanche. They green-lighted a broad Russian sanctions package to help Ukraine and approved a deal to fund the federal government through early December, as to avoid a shutdown, according to the Associated Press. But the Senate did not advance Trump’s Save America Act, which would place restrictions on voting across the US, prior to their break. Trump had pushed senators to remain in session so they could approve this proof-of-citizenship voting legislation. According to the AP, GOP senators pitched an alternative plan to Trump late on Friday. Under the Republican senators’ proposal, they would push for approval of some portions of this bill “as part of a broader GOP budget package to fund the Iran war and replenish the Pentagon when they return to work in September”. Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread throughout his body, causing the former president great pain, his son Hunter Biden said during an interview broadcast Friday. “The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden said in a sit-down with the BBC. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.” “It’s really sad to watch,” Hunter Biden also said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.” Biden, now 83, disclosed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, just months after he departed the White House. As the oldest president in US history, Biden’s age was routinely the target of his political opponents. Biden and his staff have also been criticized for purportedly hiding his health problems. This criticism came to a crux following a devastating debate against Donald Trump that prompted calls for him to step out of the presidential race. Biden abandoned his run and his vice-president, Kamala Harris, became the Democratic candidate. Donald Trump bested Harris in the election and he is serving a second term as president. Hunter Biden noted that his father has not stepped back from public life, discussing issues that matter to him. “He’s still doing his thing,” Hunter Biden said. “He so believes in this country.” Hunter Biden also remarked that he was “the most privileged person there is” after Joe Biden pardoned him. He felt that the pardon was “not good” for the nation, his father’s legacy or the US constitution. But, Hunter Biden said, he did not discuss the pardon beforehand with his father. He told the BBC that his dad did so – despite vowing not to intervene in Hunter’s criminal cases – out of fear that Donald Trump would go after him. With reporting from the Associated Press Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefl…

title: Private pensions are a publicly subsidised gift to the wealthy
summary: John Healey should equalise the tax break on pension savings to stop inequalities from widening
body: Private pensions are a privilege for the lucky few and a curse for everyone else. Sold as a saviour for what would otherwise be a ruinous old age, they have become pernicious financial vehicles that allow an older generation to hoodwink younger generations, who also seek security in their latter years. To make matters worse, saving by the better off is enhanced by state subsidies, widening the divide between rich and poor in retirement while driving a wedge between the generations. As John Healey scours the public finances for ways to boost spending on defence, social care (and the rest) before the autumn budget, he should put considering equalising the tax break on pension savings top of his list. Do standard-rate taxpayers know that they get half the subsidy for pension saving that higher-rate taxpayers receive? Probably not. Official figures published last month show that the cost of income tax relief on pensions soared from £48bn in 2022-23 to £60bn in 2024-25, an increase of a quarter in just two years. About £40bn is swallowed up by higher-rate taxpayers. That’s because higher earners get a 40% tax break while everyone else gets 20%. At the heart of the problem, and why Healey will find it difficult to confront, is the concept of retirement itself, the purpose of which has changed dramatically over the past 80 years. Once a safety net for later life when workers and carers were too infirm or too ill to continue caring or working, it has become something that should involve three, four or five holidays a year, and last for 35 years or more. It’s why many of the people standing outside pubs on a Thursday evening – a ritual Westminster council would ban – are grey heads celebrating their early retirement, and a long one to boot. Someone aged 60 in the UK will live, on average, to 84 and have a 33% chance of living to 90, according to the Office for National Statistics’ life expectancy calculator. And that predicted lifespan is longer the more affluent you are. There is a growth industry among consultants who not only plan the finances of those who retire with big pension pots, but also design a life for those who were senior in some way in the latter part of their working life and feel lost without anything to do. While many people will devote their retirement to charity work or looking after children, for too many living the retirement dream is to inhabit a comfortable cocoon. Why? Because those who have saved deserve another entire lifetime of R&R after so much hard graft, they say. Of course, those people who have actually grafted tend to have meagre pension provision. White-collar workers, and especially those in management or aged over 50, have the best of it. The scandal of baby boomers and gen Xers hoarding their pension savings can be seen in the industrial disputes of the 2010s, when almost every strike was called to defend the pensions of older workers. Shop stewards, mostly over the age of 50, would negotiate deals with managers in a similar age bracket to secure guaranteed defined benefit pensions for themselves while younger workers and new joiners were offered the much cheaper, stock market-dependent defined contribution schemes. Over time, these shop stewards and their contemporaries on both sides of the management divide have walked off into the sunset, taking their gold-plated pensions with them. It is damaging to the economy when so many experienced and skilled workers prefer buying an even bigger SUV and a cruise ship holiday to finding a way to contribute into their old age, at least while they have their health. This is especially true in a society like the UK where, since Nigel Lawson’s reforms in the 1980s, pension provision is largely privatised. Global studies of state pensions show they encourage workers to stay employed for longer, either because the payout is too low to sustain a decent standard of living, or because governments have “moved the goalposts” and delayed the state pension age. However, as the state pension has faded into insignificance for many better-off workers, the incentive changes. A defined benefit scheme, more commonly referred to as a final salary pension, has a default retirement age of 60 and anyone who has accrued all their rights has little incentive to carry on. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that those people with the lowest and highest wealth are least likely to be in work aged 65; the lowest due mainly to ill health and a lack of skills, the better off because they have lucked out with their pensions. Chief among the winners these days – those with guaranteed pensions linked to their salary rather than to the stock market – are public sector workers. They regularly attended retirement parties for colleagues who think it reasonable to retire at 60 after 35 years of office life with a pension lasting another 35, believing the failed economics of this outcome is someone else’s problem. Professional baby boomers may have escaped with their winnings to live the high life, but Healey can stop gen Xers perpetrating the same heist. Of course there will be complaints. But the judges, doctors, marketing executives and company directors who will shout loudest should ask themselves why 40% of their pension pot should be provided by other taxpayers, most of whom are much poorer than they are.

title: Nicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailed
summary: Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds
body: Nicola Surgeon has said she will not visit her estranged husband, Peter Murrell, in prison, has stopped speaking to him and views herself as a “mug” for worrying about his wellbeing and mental health earlier this year. During a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe, Scotland’s former first minister said Murrell had lied to her until the day he pleaded guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the Scottish National party. He was imprisoned for five years in June, and Sturgeon revealed she had not spoken to him since then. She told the broadcaster Iain Dale she had only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before he appeared in court. She later found out he had been negotiating his plea for months. “[That] hit me like a tonne of bricks,” she said. “He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty.” She added: “He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn’t communicative, I was a bit worried about his wellbeing and his mental health. “And then, now I think: ‘What a mug, why were you worried about him?’ He didn’t worry about me. He didn’t worry at all about what he was doing. “What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended. I don’t understand why he did it, he had no need to do it. I don’t think I will ever understand his motivations. “But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me. But I was, until recently, still worrying about him.” Asked if she would visit him in prison, Sturgeon replied: “No. I’m not going to speak to him, I’m not going to visit him.” The former first minister said that when Murrell was in court she was still finding out details of the purchases he had made using party funds. “Over the years, he never really levelled with me,” she said. “The day he pled guilty, I was still learning about some of the detail of what he had done for the first time. I suddenly realised I had been living with somebody that I never really knew properly. “That’s something for me to come to terms with, and I don’t think I’m there yet, but also for my family to come to terms with. It’s a really difficult process.” Murrell, 61, spent the money on items including a motorhome, a Jaguar SUV and a VW Golf, boutique cosmetics, iPads and a pair of Lalique Feuilles salt and pepper grinders worth £2,618. Sturgeon, 55, has consistently denied knowledge of his crimes, which spanned the years 2010 to 2022, and was not charged after a police investigation. She has previously said she made an error of judgment by keeping Murrell on as SNP chief executive when she became party leader in November 2014, but refused to apologise for his crimes and denied ever “consciously” seeing the motorhome he bought and stored at her mother-in-law’s house.

title: New York authorities warn about gold bar scam targeting older adults
summary: State’s attorney general says scammers have made off with more than $100m in past two years
body: Scammers in New York have been using gold bars to steal money from victims, primarily older adults, and made off with more than $100m over the past two years, the state’s attorney general announced on Friday. The scheme starts with victims receiving a fake pop-up message that states their computer or financial account has been compromised, the press release stated. The message includes a phone number to call, and when people do, the scammers convince the victims to provide remote access to their computers, which allows them to access their financial information or online bank accounts. The victims are then directed to someone posing as law enforcement who tells them that their accounts have been compromised. To protect their money, the person says, they must withdraw it and purchase gold bars or coins and then turn them over to the authorities. The scammers tell the victims not to discuss the breach with anyone and then send couriers to collect the gold. “Targeting older adults with seemingly legitimate claims that their life savings are in immediate danger is flat-out cruel,” the state attorney general, Letitia James, said. “Seniors deserve to live comfortably without fear of losing their hard-earned savings to a manipulative scam. I am urging all New Yorkers to beware of these gold bar scams and report suspicious messages related to this scam to my office.” The scam is not unique to New York. Victims in Hawaii, Maine, Washington DC and Wisconsin have reported the same thing happening to them. In one case in July, scammers targeted an 85-year-old man in DC by email and phone claiming to be US federal agents, and told him his money was at risk and to protect it by buying gold, ABC-7 News in DC reported. When the victim tried to purchase $200,000 in gold from a dealer, the seller recognized the scam and alerted law enforcement. The investigators then arrested the suspects when they arrived at the victim’s home to collect the gold. The attorney general instructed the public not to call a number provided in a pop-up, text or email and not to provide anyone they don’t know remote access to their computer. Individuals also should not provide money from a bank account at the urging of someone over the phone. If someone claims there is an issue with a bank account, the potential victim should contact their financial institution. Anyone concerned they may have been a victim of this scam are urged to contact law enforcement. “A scam is effective because the scammer creates a false sense of urgency, pressuring the victim into life-altering decisions on the spot and swearing them to secrecy,” the announcement stated. “The best way to combat this is to hang up and contact someone you trust and let them know your situation.”

title: Unmasked: the doctor who helps put prisoners to death
summary: Dr Mark Fowler assisted in the failed execution of a Tennessee prisoner. Physicians are meant to heal patients - why is he working in the death chamber?
body: Mark Fowler, a physician with 25 years’ experience, stepped beneath the bright lights and approached the middle-aged man lying on a gurney. Around him, people in medical gowns prepared needles and sterile tubing. It had all the appearances of a hospital setting. Fowler had been called in to help establish an IV line through which the 57-year-old man, Tony Carruthers, would be injected with pharmaceutical drugs. The team had struggled to find a vein, so Fowler was summoned to set a central line – an intravenous catheter inserted into the major vein below the collarbone. First, he had to numb the area where he would cut Carruthers with a scalpel and then pierce the vein with a large needle. But before he applied the lidocaine, he asked the IV team if “the patient” was allergic. It was a strange choice of words. Carruthers was not a patient, and the room was not an OR. Fowler had entered the death chamber at Riverbend maximum security prison in Nashville, Tennessee. Carruthers, condemned to death for a triple murder in 1994 for which there was no forensic evidence and over which he has always maintained his innocence, was forcibly strapped to the gurney. The tube Fowler was attempting to insert would pipe the sedative pentobarbital at a lethally high dose. Standing just a few feet away inside the chamber was Carruthers’ lawyer, Maria DeLiberato, a senior counsel at the ACLU’s capital punishment project. She heard the doctor’s description of her client, and recoiled. “He called Tony ‘the patient’,” she said. “And he was trying to kill him.” *** Mark Walton Fowler, 68, of Union City, Tennessee, is an exceedingly rare breed: a doctor who signed up to participate in executions, and whose identity has become public. In most cases, execution physicians are shielded by ironclad secrecy laws, allowing them to carry out their controversial work shrouded in anonymity. Fowler has not been so lucky. He was identified, paradoxically, by the Tennessee department of corrections. A warden inadvertently let slip his name as he announced the death by lethal injection of another death row prisoner, Byron Black, 69, last August. The public disclosure has clearly inconvenienced Fowler. Two months after his name was released, he was subpoenaed by lawyers acting for prisoners challenging the constitutionality of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. In the course of the deposition, an irritated Fowler scolded his inquisitors. “I certainly hope your office will handle this responsibly,” he chided, “and that I won’t be reading about myself in the Nashville Banner or the Guardian.” Before Fowler could read about himself in the Guardian, I called him on his cell phone. He declined to respond to a list of detailed questions, but he did say that this was “a private situation. The inmate is entitled to privacy. The lawyers are churning up a lot of nonsense, and I don’t want to discuss it.” The inconvenient truth, however, is that Fowler’s situation is no longer private. It has erupted into public debate about the death penalty and Tennessee’s record in applying it. *** The botched procedure placed Carruthers in his own rare category: people who have survived an execution attempt. Fowler was unable to secure the central line, and after Carruthers had spent an hour and 15 minutes being repeatedly pierced by Fowler and the IV team in his arms, feet and shoulder, the execution was called off. Next Thursday, Tennessee is scheduled to execute Darrell Hines also by lethal injection. The prisoner, 65, who was convicted of a 1985 murder, is in poor health, having suffered multiple strokes that have left him partially paralyzed. Hines’s lawyers have argued in court filings that if Fowler were to be allowed back into the death chamber for what would be his fifth execution, the same botched procedure endured by Carruthers would probably be repeated. They alleged that there would be “an intolerable risk that [Hines] will experience severe suffering due to the … use of insufficiently qualified medical personnel”. On Thursday, the Tennessee supreme court denied a motion that would have obliged the state to disclose whether the physician will be on duty next week. That means he is now likely to disappear back into the shadows. At a more fundamental level, Fowler’s unmasking has laid bare the ethical conundrum at the heart of lethal injections, America’s killing technique of choice for the past 44 years. From its inception, the protocol has been wrapped in the swaddling clothes of medicine. It was billed as the humane answer to the primitive brutality of the electric chair or the firing squad. But to meet such claims, death penalty states have had to persuade doctors to participate – and there’s the rub. For 2,500 years doctors have operated under the Hippocratic Oath, with its soaring edict: “Do no harm.” The following line of the oath is less well known, but for these purposes even more instructive: “To please no one will I prescribe a deadly drug, nor give advice which may cause his death.” In 1980, two years before Charles Brooks in Texas became the first prisoner to be killed by lethal injection in the US, the American Medical Association issued a clear prohibition: “A physician must not participate in a legally authorized execution.” As Corinna Lain has chronicled in her book, Secrets of the Killing State, that has whittled down the field of physicians available to death penalty states to a rump of those Lain calls the “dissenters” – doctors ethically flexible or contrarian enough to bring their white coats and healing arts into the death chamber. And as we now know from the warden’s slip of the tongue, Fowler is one of them. *** The road that led Fowler to Riverbend, Tennessee is long and winding. He studied public administration at the University of Tennessee (UT), then went into law. Long before he became involved in executions, Fowler spent three years as a public defender. He even represented several capital defendants, managing in each case to persuade the jury to spare his client a death sentence. Around 1994 Fowler made a dramatic career switch, retraining to become a doctor at the UT Memphis college of medicine. The yearbook of his 1999 graduating class shows him wearing a gown and glasses, smiling broadly. His appearance chimes with the description given by someone who has worked alongside Fowler: “He looks like the kind of fella who goes on fishing trips in Alabama and drinks beer.” In a quarter century of medical practice Fowler has tried his hand at several different aspects of the profession. For the first decade or so he worked as an ER physician, then as a family doctor. Today, most of his income comes through numerous medical directorships, including of weight loss and aesthetic clinics, and a wound care facility. There have been controversies along the way. In the deposition he said his employment ended at Centurion, the company that provides healthcare services to Tennessee’s prisons, after he engaged colleagues in a conversation about a transgender prisoner in a women’s prison in Connecticut whom he claimed had impregnated two other women. We don’t know precisely what Fowler said, but it was provocative enough to inspire a formal complaint from the prison psychiatrist who overheard it. Fowler writes occasional opinion columns for his local newspaper, the Union City Daily Messenger, that are reproduced by the conservative blog the Patriot Post. The articles give a glimpse into his staunchly rightwing, Trumpian worldview – a way of thinking whose proponents often advocate for the death penalty and have proposed reverting to older, brutal methods such as “firing squads”. After Renee Good and Alex Pretti were shot dead in Minneapolis in January by federal officers amid Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, Fowler wrote that they had been “killed because they and others were violent and/or reckless” (neither victim engaged the officials in violence). In February he penned a column that accused liberals of condoning violence. He wrote that “liberal logic” dictated that “Christian conservatives must be shut out of public discourse by killing them (Charlie Kirk)”. In a column from June 2025 he addressed his previous life as a public defender. “I managed a number of death penalty cases in my career. None got the death penalty, although two cases come to mind where it was surely warranted,” he wrote. In the same article, he recognised that there could be lapses in a criminal justice system in which overzealous prosecutors, “corrupt police”, and “prosecution-oriented judges” can be thrown together. The result can be that “the constitutional protections intended to protect individuals from erroneous convictions are watered down to nothing”. *** In the course of last October’s deposition, Fowler related how he came to sign up as Tennessee’s execution doctor. Under the state’s official protocol, he is assigned the responsibility for setting a central line if necessary, and at the end of the procedure he must determine that the prisoner is dead. Fowler said that he was a friend of the state’s previous death penalty physician. In 2018, “he asked me to accompany him to an execution so that I might take over when he retired.” That rather bland narrative illuminates little as to motive. Could it be the money? During the deposition it was revealed that Fowler is paid $3,000 for every execution he attends, well below what he might command in other states such as Oklahoma ($15,000) and Arizona ($18,000). When asked about the payments, Fowler grew tetchy. “I don’t wish to read about myself in the newspaper saying, ‘This bloodthirsty coward doctor gets money for doing this.’ I get paid for the time and effort of going.” Further insight can be gleaned from an interview he gave NBC News shortly after the failed Carruthers execution. “Every attempt was made to minimize the defendant’s discomfort,” Fowler said. “No one wants Carruthers to suffer.” But Carruth…

title: Bar fight: Hugo cocktail takes aim at Aperol in UK summer of spritz
summary: The elderflower drink is enjoying explosive growth, with Campari, Sarti Rosa and limoncello varieties also taking off
body: It’s the summer of spritz as British sales figures show the Hugo elderflower cocktail snapping at the heels of the market-leader Aperol to be this year’s favourite drink. The number of Hugos ordered in bars nearly tripled in the three months to the end of June while demand for the vibrant red Campari spritz surged 52%. A limoncello version has also taken off, with sales up 31%, according to the payments company Square. The Hugo “has absolutely blown up,” said Steve Young, business unit director for Bacardi in the UK (the group’s St-Germain liqueur is the drink’s signature ingredient). He agreed that the Hugo spritz could be the drink of summer. Young said sales of St-Germain are growing faster in the UK than in any other country, with the elderflower liqueur “outselling some of our major spritz competitors across a lot of our customers. It has doubled in size over the last 12 months.” Created in Italy, and very popular in France, the Hugo is sweeter than an Aperol spritz and is made with elderflower liqueur, prosecco, soda water and mint. The spritz sales data, gleaned from bar, cafe and restaurant till receipts, showed a 196% uplift for the Hugo in Great Britain in the three months to the end of June compared with a year ago. For the same period, Aperol spritz sales climbed 13%. The phenomenon is driven in part by the rise of the “daycap” – a replacement for the traditional nightcap with a longer, lighter-tasting drink in the late afternoon. This coincides with a shift in drinking patterns as late-afternoon – as opposed to late-night – drinking has become popular with millennials and gen Z. But it is gen Z that has put a rocket under the spritz business. For this age group (18-29) it is the number one cocktail, despite ranking sixth overall, according to Bacardi’s annual cocktail trends report. The popularity of the spritz means the choice on bar menus is increasing. This has been good news for Campari, which owns a drinks cabinet full of brands suitable for making colourful, Instagram-friendly spritzes. In the UK, sales of the group’s aperitif brands – which include Aperol, Campari, Sarti Rosa and the non-alcoholic Crodino – were up more than 10% in the first six months of this year. With its notes of “blood orange, mango and passion fruit”, the hot pink Sarti spritz is tipped as the next big thing, with Google searches up 341% on 2025. “The spritz has taken the UK by storm,” said Young. “Two years ago it did not make the top 10 in our annual survey and now it is the number one choice for gen-Zers.” But it is not just on a night out that Britons are enjoying a spritz, as supermarket and high street sales data suggests they have been added to the drinks cabinets of those socialising at home. “Spritzes are having their moment this summer,” said Tom Oakton, analyst at the data company NielsenIQ, adding that sales of this type of cocktail were growing much faster than the alcohol market as a whole in the UK. “Aperol remains the most popular, but St-Germain saw triple-digit growth from the rising popularity of the Hugo spritz,” said Oakton. While Aperol sales were up 32.4% by value in the 12 weeks to 1 August – boosted by the launch of Aperol-in-a-tin – St-Germain grew 135.5%. Francesca Parker-Partridge, spirits buyer at Ocado Retail, confirmed that spritzes are “dominating this summer’s drink scene. Total liqueur sales are up 19% year on year, driven by a massive 122% spike for St-Germain.” The Hugo may be elbowing its way on to drinks menus, but it still has a way to go to steal Aperol’s crown, with St-Germain becoming the David to the bright orange Goliath. Industry data suggests that about eight Aperols are sold for every St-Germain mixed Hugo. “It’s great to see new brands joining the space and growing the category, but scale tells the real story, with 8.8m cases sold globally last year alone,” said Francesco Cruciani, the managing director of Campari Group UK. “The Campari group remains the undisputed trailblazer leading the spritz movement into its next era,” he added, in comments underlining that – for the time being at least – Aperol is still king of the spritzes.

title: Who’s winning New York City’s war on rats: rodents or trash bins?
summary: City on track to record fewest reported rat sightings since pandemic as Mamdani’s ‘containerization’ program brings bins to boroughs
body: Is New York finally winning its war on rats? Or are New Yorkers’ vermin neighbors merely adapting to changing circumstances and, at least in some neighborhoods, staying out of sight? With an estimated one rat for every three people, New York’s long-running rat war is in a period of uneasy detente. Last week Bloomberg reported that New York is on track to record the fewest reported rat sightings since the pandemic, down 22% in the first seven months of 2026 compared to a year earlier, a drop attributed to a “war on rats” campaign initiated by former mayor Eric Adams. The city’s population had spiked during the Coivd pandemic when rats flourished unchecked due to uncollected trash, an increase in take-out and delivery food, and outdoor dining sheds that provided snacks and refuge. As mayor, Adams was fixated on rats. His administration posted an advertisement for a “rat czar” that would require applicants to be “highly motivated and somewhat bloodthirsty” and possessed of both “stamina and stagecraft” and a “swashbuckling attitude, crafty humor and general aura of badassery”. When Adams appointed Kathleen Corradi to the post in early 2023, he said sagely: “Rats impact how you feel about the city you’re in … many of us live in communities where rats think they run the city.” The measures Adams’ instituted included “Rat Pack” teams, a bin program that Adams called the city’s “trash revolution” requiring trash cans throughout the five boroughs to reduce household waste left on the streets for collection in plastic trash bags. During his tenure, Adams ordered the formation of specialized teams to tackle the estimated 600,000 rats that live in the city’s street tree beds. Thousands live in holes in the city parks, venturing out only at night to feed on trash. All businesses and low-density residential buildings, producers of around 70% of the city’s trash, were required to containerize in 2024. Full containerization of the city’s trash is expected to be complete by 2031. Leading rodentologist Robert Corrigan said he felt “very positive” about the containerization effort. He told Bloomberg that garbage is a rat’s favorite food and lids on trash cans are “the true hero of rat management”. The first concerted effort to tackle the issue came in late 2022 when Adams and then-Sanitation commissioner Jessica Tisch launched a “Get Stuff Clean” initiative, cleaning up neglected areas and combatting litter. Tisch was asked if a sanitation department flyer featuring a travel influencer rat with a suitcase was too cute. Tisch said the point was to get people’s attention. “Everyone that knows me, they know one thing: I hate rats,” Adams told reporters when the city narrowed the window when trash can be put out on the curb. He acknowledged that he’d be branded a murderer. “Well, you know what? We’re going to kill rats.” The current mayor, Zohran Mamdani, does not appear to share Adams obsession with rats. He dropped the “rat czar” position but has expanded the city’s “containerization” program to six districts, bringing oversize “Empire Bins” to 25,000 new residences. The city is set to lose 30,000 parking spots as a result, alongside a city council proposal threatening up to 300,000 spots. “In the wealthiest city in the wealthiest nation in the history of the world, no New Yorker should have their sidewalks covered in garbage. By finishing the job on containerization, we will ensure New York City’s streets remain the envy of the world,” said Mamdani said in April. But is it really as simple as that? Not all of the city’s neighborhoods have seen the same improvements. West Harlem, which as been fully containerized since June 2025, reported rat sightings fell 34% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with last year. Though overall rat sightings are down so far this year, it’s not uniform across community districts. Parts of Brooklyn’s Dumbo and Brooklyn Heights are down 48%. But the gentrified East Village, Lower East Side and parts of Chinatown have seen a 37% surge in rodent reports compared to this time last year. Overall numbers of rats, or rat sightings, have dropped, but they are not below pre-Covid levels, suggesting that the New Yorker’s furry frenemies are still very much in situ despite the loss of Covid dining sheds and easy-to-access refuse. Gil Bloom of Standard Pest Management, a company that consults for local and federal government agencies, says rat sightings dropped to a record low in 2019. “Covid rearranged the topography and rats went wild. They were running around horribly once we had these food shacks up all around the city and the population skyrocketed.” Bloom says the city’s rat population has certainly gone down with trash containerization, but warns it would be unwise to declare victory given the adaptability of rodents. “We have to consider who our adversary is,” he says. “They’re still in the underground and catch spaces of the city.” With some trash still in bags, and the time between trash being left out and collected, rats “have reset their clocks. They know when the trash is going out. People litter. There are food and fruit stands. There’s still enough food around for rodents to survive.” While the visibility of rats has been reduced that doesn’t necessarily reflect the total number. New Yorkers relationship to rats, like many attributes of city life, is psychological bordering on metaphysical. “If they’re out at night and people don’t see them is it still a rat? It’s still a rat, but no one is seeing it,” Bloom says. The East Village has older buildings, the large Tompkins Square Park and city infrastructure in disrepair below ground. Plus it has a younger population more likely to be out at night. Parks don’t used rodenticide because of the hawks and birds, but use traps with liquid nitrogen to freeze the holes. The variables are endless, Bloom says. “Rats are burrowing animals and in a city with limited earth and space, a rat is going to find you. We’ve learned over the last 15 or 20 years that a rats’ range is much greater than we previously thought,” he says. “ Rats only require one ounce of food and water a day, they don’t need a whole sandwich. “So there’s a direction toward control, and the numbers are down to pre-Covid levels. But pre-Covid there were still a lot of rats, so no one is saying, ‘Hey, there’s no rats,’”

title: Lion saved as cub from Ukraine war and brought to US battles rare fungal disease
summary: Four-year-old Taras, who now resides at a Minnesota sanctuary, was diagnosed with an often fatal infection
body: A lion that escaped the war in Ukraine after being found as a four-month-old cub inside a duffel bag at Odesa railway station is facing an even greater battle for survival in his new home in Minnesota from a rare and often fatal fungal disease. Taras, his two sisters Lesya and Stefania, and an unrelated, slightly older cub from Kyiv named Prada, were brought to the US in November 2022 by the Wildcat Sanctuary, a secluded private reserve near Sandstone, Minnesota, that arranged their rescue with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW). An American veterinarian working in Ukraine’s capital, which was under sporadic attack from Russian missiles and drones, evacuated them from Kyiv to safety in Poland, a 36-hour land journey, where they awaited import permits for the US. Now, aged four, Taras was an energetic head of the Ukrainian pride until May, when veterinarians noticed he was sluggish and off his food. Numerous tests, including a 180-mile round trip for an expensive scan and lung biopsy at a specialist clinic in Minneapolis, diagnosed blastomycosis, a non-contagious fungal infection usually contracted from soil. The condition was blamed in the death of a white tiger called Ginger at a wildlife sanctuary in Wisconsin in June. Also known as Gilchrist’s disease, it is often fatal in humans and animals if not caught early and treated. Tammy Thies, the sanctuary’s founder and chief executive, said Taras responded well to intensive treatment, including twice daily injections of extra strength anti-fungal medication through an IV line in the early weeks, and had rejoined his pride. But he still requires oral medicine twice a day, she said, and it could still be weeks or months before sanctuary staff could be confident he was out of the woods. “He was in a fight for his life,” she said. “Usually when big cats are diagnosed with blastomycosis it’s when they’re showing respiratory distress, and by that time the disease is so advanced that even the aggressive antifungal medication can be life-threatening. There’s a very low chance of survival. “The specialist told us he had a guarded prognosis, and when I asked, ‘does he have a 30% chance?’, they all just looked at me and looked at their feet. We knew this was going to be an uphill battle, and we might not be able to save him.” Thies said Taras’s survival was his “second miracle”, after escaping the Ukraine war with his siblings. “Everybody we reached out to just told us they were sorry and not to be optimistic,” she said. “We’re just really grateful for the staff and the vet team that found this early, before he was showing breathing symptoms, because I don’t think we could have saved him.” His reunion with his sisters was emotional. “He wanted to be with his family, so we started with one play date with a sister at a time,” she said. “We were concerned that after being away for weeks they could pick on him [but] there was so much nuzzling going on, and so much rolling around on each other, the pride welcomed him with open arms, and they’ve been inseparable ever since.” Even so, Taras still needs to be separated twice every day so his pride members do not steal his food with the medication in it. The lions’ origin is impossible to know, Thies said, but they were likely taken from their mother after birth and destined to become part of the illegal but lucrative international trade in exotic animals, at least until the start of the war thwarted the smugglers’ plans. “As borders were getting shut down and checkpoints set up, a lot of these traffickers were dumping the animals versus trying to smuggle them across the border to sell them,” she said. “It was just devastating after all he went through, after this lion had fought so hard and come out so much stronger, to then get a diagnosis of a fungal disease in his lungs, and to know he might not make it. “That was the hardest for us. He has a fight on his hands but still has a lot of life to live, and we were all going to come together and fight for him.”

title: Trump loyalist Todd Blanche confirmed by Senate as US attorney general
summary: Major win for president as former personal lawyer wins approval despite outcry over $1.8bn slush fund
body: The US Senate voted to narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a major win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor after two other Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – voted against him. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination as the Republican-led Senate voted 50-49. Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity, and the vote came after his nomination had been in limbo for weeks. He faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons and his businesses tax immunity. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said Friday on the Senate floor announcing his decision. “It is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” The Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said Senate Republicans have “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general. “If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,” he wrote in a post on X. “Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.” Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me”, adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him. Concern around the “anti-weaponization fund” appears to have cost Blanche among at least some GOP senators who opposed his nomination, including Murkowski. “I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund – which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters – is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” Murkowski said in a post on X on Friday, announcing she was voting against Blanche. But John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina successfully pushed Blanche to put in writing that the fund was not moving forward and to clarify the scope of the IRS deal. Even though experts said the assurances were far from ironclad, Cornyn and Tillis wound up supporting Blanche, allowing his nomination to narrowly clear the Senate judiciary committee. Blanche also faced heavy criticism for the department’s sloppy rollout of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, which redacted information that should not have been redacted and left unredacted the names of victims that should have been kept private. During his confirmation hearing, Blanche refused to personally meet with Epstein victims, then agreed to do so. The survivors said they received few answers from Blanche during the meeting. Blanche, who left a lucrative partnership to represent Trump in 2023, has been at the center of the president’s attempt to bend the federal government to his will. Scores of career justice department attorneys have left the agency under his leadership. Department lawyers have been rebuked by judges across the US for making misrepresentations to the court. Blanche has also been at the center of Trump’s efforts to use the justice department to punish political rivals. During his tenure as both the deputy attorney general and acting attorney general, the department has indicted former FBI director James Comey twice; the New York attorney general, Letitia James; and the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center – all in cases that exerts see as thin. It has also tried to bring criminal charges against two Democratic senators, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and used its investigative powers to try and get leverage over Jerome Powell, the former chairman of the Federal Reserve. “The Attorney General should serve the American people, not the president’s wish list,” Kelly said in a statement on Saturday in which he also noted that Blanche “met with Ghislane Maxwell in secret” before the convicted Epstein accomplice was transferred to a minimum-security prison camp. Blanche, Kelly added “is defined by his loyalty to Trump”. As his nomination was pending, Blanche also promised anti-abortion advocates the department would make the Dobbs decision permanent in every state, according to Politico. “While I believe Mr Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins, who is running for re-election in Maine, said earlier this week. “Mr Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation.” Earlier this year, Blanche spoke about how he would feel if someone else was named attorney general. “As to whether or not I want this job, I did not ask for this job. I love working for President Trump, it’s the greatest honor of a lifetime,” he said in April, shortly after being named the acting attorney general. “If he chooses to nominate somebody else and asks me to go do something else, I will say, ‘Thank you very much. I love you, sir.’ I don’t have any goals or aspirations beyond that.”

title: Senate passes funding bill to prevent shutdown through US midterms
summary: Bill must still be approved by House but would keep government running at current funding levels
body: The US Senate on Friday passed a government funding bill that will prevent a shutdown through the midterm elections, though it still must be approved by the House of Representatives. The continuing resolution (CR) passed by a 90-6 vote will keep the government running at its current funding levels until 11 December, more than a month past the midterms in which Democrats are hoping to regain control of Congress and block Donald Trump’s legislative agenda for the final two years of his presidency. The measure’s passage signals a recognition by both parties that they would prefer to avoid a messy battle over federal spending in the weeks leading up to the 3 November vote. The government will shut down after 30 September if new funding is not approved, and the Republican Senate appropriations committee chair, Susan Collins, called the CR “a major step toward averting a damaging shutdown that only harms vital programs and federal workers”, and noted it makes no major changes to funding levels. The House had last month approved a different CR that would continue funding until 4 December. It is unclear which bill will ultimately be adopted – the House is on recess until the end of the month, and senators were expected to leave Washington DC for their break following the vote. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate appropriations committee, said the House’s bill had “several major issues” that the Senate’s version addressed. It would block until 11 December a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats fear would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. The Senate CR also closes what Murray called a “loophole” in the House bill that would have allowed the White House to take money meant for other purposes and give it to the border patrol. “Today’s CR gives us the breathing room necessary to work out a budget that helps make life more affordable to working families and reins in Trump’s rampant chaos, his rampant corruption,” the Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, said ahead of the vote. Democrats instigated a government shutdown last year when they refused to approve funding bills without an agreement to extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push, then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

title: Super-rich complain but experts welcome Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax
summary: New York mayor’s policy set to generate revenue and address housing crisis despite outcry in some quarters
body: New York City’s introduction of a pied-à-terre tax has provided fodder for Zohran Mamdani’s critics, who accuse the democratic socialist mayor of attacking the rich – even as others welcome it as a much-needed effort to tax the wealthy in a city known for its yawning inequality and cost-of-living crisis. The tax, aimed at closing the city’s budget gap, covers people who own but do not live full-time in a house worth more than $5m or a condominium or cooperative unit worth at least $1m.
